title: Informal Letters: Writing to People Who Know You

blocks.text: "I wish to state categorically that the aforementioned excursion was highly beneficial to my person." Every word is correct English. But the writer was addressing his cousin, and no cousin has ever spoken like that. Register — matching your language to your reader — is what the informal letter tests.

blocks.markdown:
An **informal** or **friendly letter** goes to someone with whom you have a personal relationship: a parent, a sibling, a cousin, a friend, a former classmate.

Because the reader already knows who you are and where you live, the letter needs far less machinery than a formal one. What it does need is a voice that sounds like you.

rows: Dear Mum / Dear Uncle Emeka / Dear Chidi
Your loving son / Yours affectionately / Love

blocks.title: Do not import formal features
blocks.text: The three commonest format faults are adding the recipient's address, adding an underlined heading, and closing with *Yours faithfully*. Each of these belongs to the official letter, and each signals to the examiner that the candidate has not identified the letter type.

blocks.markdown:
### What informal register allows

- **Contractions**: *I'm*, *don't*, *can't*, *it's*
- **Direct questions**: *How have you been?* *Did your father recover?*
- **Exclamations**, used sparingly: *You will not believe what happened!*
- **Everyday vocabulary**: *tell*, not *inform*; *ask*, not *make enquiries*
- **Greetings to third parties**: *Do greet your parents for me.*

### What it still forbids

- Pidgin, slang and text-message spelling
- Faulty grammar, concord and punctuation
- Paragraphs that ramble with no clear subject

Informal is not the same as careless. The letter is still assessed for content, organisation, expression and mechanical accuracy.

blocks.title: Planning an informal letter
blocks.prompt: Write to your cousin in Enugu telling her about your school's inter-house sports and inviting her to visit during the holiday.

steps.text: Lay out the six features: your address top right, the date under it, salutation, body, warm close, first name. Do not add anything else.
Choose the salutation to match the relationship: *Dear Ngozi*.
Paragraph one: greet her, apologise for the silence if there has been any, and say why you are writing now.
Paragraph two: tell the story of the inter-house sports with concrete detail — which house won, what went wrong with the relay, who fell in the mud.
Paragraph three: make the invitation specific. Give dates, say who else will be around and what you plan to do together.
Close warmly: send greetings to her family, ask her to reply soon, then *Yours affectionately* and your first name.
Reread for register. Replace any office language — *kindly note*, *aforementioned*, *in this regard* — with the words you would actually say to her.

blocks.answer: Three body paragraphs — greeting and purpose, the news told with concrete detail, the specific invitation — inside the six-feature informal format.

items: To a parent: *Dear Mum* / *Dear Dad*, closing *Your loving son* or *Your loving daughter*.
To an older relative: *Dear Uncle Emeka*, closing *Yours affectionately*.
To a friend of your own age: *Dear Chidi*, closing *Yours sincerely*, *Your friend* or *Love*.
Sign off with your first name only — a friend does not need your surname.
Keep to three or four paragraphs, each with one clear subject.

blocks.title: WAEC and NECO tip
blocks.text: Before writing a single word, ask yourself: who is the reader? If the reader is somebody who knows you personally, drop the recipient's address and the heading immediately. Candidates who confuse the two formats lose marks they could have kept with one moment of thought.

points: An informal letter carries only the writer's address, and no subject heading.
The salutation names the reader as you actually address them.
Subscriptions are warm: *Your loving son*, *Yours affectionately*, *Love*.
Sign off with your first name only.
Informal register allows contractions, questions and everyday words.
Informal does not mean careless: pidgin, slang and grammatical errors are still penalised.
